Environment Agency says talks under way about increasing prices for industrial users to try to reduce poor water management




Ministers are exploring making water more expensive for some users, in the face of severe supply shortages.
Despite the UK being a famously wet country, the precarious nature of the water supply has been made particularly acute this summer, with almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales in drought and 27 million people facing restrictions on their water use.

As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agency has estimated that, without action, England’s water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055.
Helen Wakeham, the director of water at the Environment Agency, said that to plug this severe and growing gap, the value of water needed to increase.


“If someone wants an abstraction licence from the Environment Agency, what they pay for is the cost of producing the licence. They don’t pay anything towards the value of that water,” she said.
While millions of households in England are paying record levels for their water bills, Wakeham said that, for big industrial customers, the more water they used, the less they paid.
There was a “lively conversation” going on about whether we could “completely reframe the way we value and pay for water”.
“It’s the beginning of a conversation, but ministers have asked us to look at the value of water and how our abstraction licensing system works,” she said.
The Guardian recently revealed that less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people. Some of these businesses, which include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, face no requirements to cut their consumption.
With the government committed to make England an AI superpower, there are also questions about where water-hungry datacentres will get their resources from. Water UK, the body representing the UK water industry, warned the UK would not have enough water for future datacentres.
“The reason datacentres are water-hungry is because water is so cheap,” said Wakeham.


View image in fullscreen
An aerial view of the depleted Chew reservoir in Oldham, England, in August. Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty Images


Dr Doug Parr, Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist and policy adviser, said: “Every day, people are doing their bit to save water, but they are being hit with higher bills and hosepipe bans while big business gets cheap water access. At a time when the country is facing water stress due to climate change, it is absurd that major companies have access to water that is cheaper for them, per litre, the more they use. This has to change. The whole abstraction policy and licensing needs to be rewritten from a blank sheet of paper to make it fit for a country facing summer droughts and a biodiversity crisis.”

articles.raw_rss: It's a journey time of just 60 minutes.
articles.raw_content:
The airline is facing some backlash for their new domestic flight route (Picture: Getty Images)



From France to Turkey, Easyjet offers more than 630 routes, ferrying UK passengers to destinations across Europe and beyond.

The budget airline regularly announces new flights — just this summer, they revealed a new route to Pristina, the capital of Kosovo, as well as new flights from Bristol to Glasgow.

But now, the carrier has unveiled a domestic route that’s divided travellers.

Now available on the Easyjet website, you can book tickets between Manchester and Southampton.

Starting on December 4, just in time for Christmas, the trip covers around 170 miles (as the crow flies), each way.

It will be one of Easyjet’s shortest routes (not including those between islands), second only to the flight between Geneva and Milan Linate.


	
			
		Flights will operate on Mondays and Fridays (Picture: Shutterstock/Dimi Jeckov)



The cost to the environment

The announcement has left some eco-conscious customers asking why such a trip has been made available.

Aviation produces roughly 2.5% of the world’s carbon emissions, and is one of the most carbon-intensive forms of transport.

‘Nobody needs to fly between Manchester and Southampton,’ wrote Fiona Jade on X. ‘Literally nobody. There’s an hourly direct train!’

And user, Juo, wrote: ‘We’re in a climate crisis and airlines are doing s*** like this?’

As public air monitors disappear, federal rollbacks and state laws are making it harder than ever to know what’s in the air




As the US’s network for monitoring air pollution deteriorates, a Floodlight investigation has found that the chemical industry is going state-to-state to restrict one of the few options citizens have left for holding polluters accountable: low-cost air sensors.
Over the past two years, the non-profit investigative newsroom determined, lawmakers in Louisiana, Kentucky and Ohio have passed strikingly similar laws barring regulators from acting on air-quality data that communities collect themselves – unless it comes from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-approved equipment that typically costs tens of thousands of dollars. Similar legislation has repeatedly been introduced in West Virginia.



View image in fullscreen
A California official calibrates rooftop air monitoring equipment used to track local air pollution. Photograph: Dave Clegern/Photo courtesy of the California Air Resources Board
In case after case, industry has made the same argument: community monitoring is not reliable enough for regulatory enforcement.


Yet when lawmakers in West Virginia offered a version of a bill that would have let regulators consider community data if it met manufacturer requirements, industry refused to back it.
The bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent”, wrote Jeff Fritz, an official with the chemical giant Chemours, in an internal email. Bill Bissett of the West Virginia Manufacturers Association wrote that the compromise “neuters” the measure and left it “toothless”. That bill died, along with versions in 2025 and 2026.
Ohio slipped its monitor restriction into a budget bill last year, prompting a lawsuit from a group of plaintiffs including Donna Ballinger.
Ballinger has a low-cost monitor in her front yard in Middletown, Ohio, a few hundred feet from a steel plant that she says frequently sends black, white and gray particles on to her property. Fumes sometimes burn her eyes and throat, she said, and she often holds her nose when walking between her house and car.
“My fear is cancer,” she said.
The lawsuit she helped file alleges that the new rules make her monitor’s readings useless as evidence.
An early-warning system in decline


People have turned to low-cost sensors at a time when the public network they used to rely on is thinning out. Federal grants supporting that network have fallen more than 35% over the past two decades, adjusted for inflation, and the number of government air monitors nationwide has fallen by nearly half over the same period, according to EPA data.

A scientist discusses an air-monitoring car with Louisiana Environmental Action Network staff. The Trump administration canceled the group’s air monitoring grant last year.  Photograph: Zachary Kanzler/Courtesy of the Louisiana Environmental Action Network

Climate ‘feedback loops’ could worsen global warming by 30%, study finds


Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says




Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world’s forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found.
As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and carbon dioxide locked in trees and soils, therefore worsening the climate crisis, the paper states.

While scientists have long known of these “feedback loops” that amplify the impact of direct pollution from burning coal, oil and gas, the emissions from natural sources are largely unaccounted for in climate projections.
This additional heating is however significant, researchers found, with emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century. This would add an estimated 0.2C to 0.4C to the global average temperature by this time, depending on the overall action taken by countries to combat the climate crisis.


View image in fullscreen
Fumaroles are seen in an area of cultivated cattail swamps to mitigate air pollution threat at the Salton Sea on 19 February 2021 near Calipatria, California.  Photograph: David McNew/Getty Images
Even small fractions of temperature change across the global climate can greatly change the risk of severe and deadly heatwaves, floods, drought and other impacts.


The United Nations last week conceded the international pact to constraint the global temperature rise to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels will be breached in the next few years, causing climate impacts such as this summer’s record heatwaves and wildfires to “strike faster, hit harder and last longer.”
Yet the increase in the world’s fever will likely be even larger than most projections currently account for, the new research warns, as they do not factor in the methane and CO2 that will spew from permafrost, wetlands, freshwaters and wildfires – the four areas the paper analyzed.

Temperatures for the month were 1.65C above pre-industrial levels - surpassing the critical 1.5C threshold agreed by countries to avoid the worst consequences of climate change.
While a single month above 1.5C does not mean it has been permanently crossed, it shows a trend towards breaching that limit.
The month also capped western Europe's warmest summer, with high temperatures pushing the season past the deadly heat of 2003.









Dr Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, described August as "a remarkable month in the global climate record", and its impacts had been "increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world".
The combination of record air temperatures, record ocean heat and Europe's exceptional summer showed how climate change was now driving extremes across "both the atmosphere and the oceans", she said.

"The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling," he said.
On top of the ongoing impact of the use of fossil fuels, the rise of a powerful El Niño is making matters worse, the researchers have said.
El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which a band of the eastern Pacific turns unusually warm, releasing vast amounts of stored ocean heat into the atmosphere and nudging global temperatures upwards for around a year.
The one currently being experienced is still strengthening and could become one of the most powerful on record, according to the Copernicus team.

In the first project of its kind, scientists are trying to answer if the future of Alaska’s streams and tundra may depend not on survival of the fittest but on how species adapt together

By Gloria Dickie




On Alaska’s North Slope, scientists tread carefully across clumps of tussock grasses toward a fast-flowing stream draining the imposing Brooks Range of ice and snow. Near Galbraith Creek, they string out a mist net for white-crowned sparrows. The birds have recently arrived from southerly latitudes, intent on feasting on the insects that will soon descend on the tundra like storm clouds.
The Arctic summer is short-lived, and sparrows have only a few weeks to establish territories, find mates, lay eggs and raise their chicks on a steady diet of bugs. From every ensnared bird, the scientists collect blood, feather and faecal samples to see what they are eating and how that changes over the summer.

One thing they want to know is whether the sparrows are consuming a lot of stream insects, such as stoneflies and mayflies, says Ian Shuman, a doctoral student in quantitative ecology at Columbia University. As willow shrubs claim new territory along the Arctic’s rivers and streams – a process scientists call “shrubification” – this could disrupt the life cycles of stoneflies and mayflies. If the songbirds also depend on aquatic insects to thrive, that might affect the sparrows’ prospects.
The tundra can feel immutable in its vastness. A sea of grass and moss extends as far as the eye can see. But above the Arctic Circle, change is happening faster than anywhere else on Earth. Snow is melting earlier in the spring, sending torrents of water downstream. By late summer, such early season deluges have given way to parched creek beds. The Arctic grayling – cold water fish in the salmon family – that swim between deep lake winter refuges and shallow summer spawning streams may become stranded in isolated pools. Their survival, too, rests on the mayflies and stoneflies.

The European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights projects helping people cope with climate crisis




In the words of Joni Mitchell, the planners of many urban centres around the world “paved paradise and put up a parking lot”. The European Prize for Urban Public Space tries to show that cities don’t have to be locked in the automotive age for ever.
The prize’s latest shortlist, announced on Wednesday, highlights architectural projects that convert infrastructure for cars into spaces that help urban dwellers cope with the soaring temperatures of the climate crisis: roundabouts that have become splash pools, thoroughfares turned into green havens, and car parks into gardens.

Among the most eye-catching of the five finalists is Leopold Banchini’s Round About Baths in Logroño, northern Spain. The Swiss architect’s project sought to revive what he called a “lost space” on one of the main thoroughfares in the city, a concrete island with a broken fountain.


View image in fullscreen
Round About Baths attempted to reclaim a space that would normally be out-of-bounds for those without a motor vehicle. Photograph: Josema Cutillas
Inspired by 19th-century public baths, Banchini’s studio used uncut timber panels to build and place a simple structure directly on to the fountain. The existing water basin became a shallow pool, while cast-iron flower pots were repurposed as fire bowls that heat a steam room.
“We have given up so much public space to cars, and if you live in a city with kids you live in constant fear that they will be hit by a passing vehicle”, Banchini said. “It restricts our movement so much that we almost can’t see it anymore.”
Those trying to catch a glimpse of the roundabout baths in situ will be disappointed, however: Banchini’s structure was only erected for a week as part of the city’s Concéntrico architecture festival in June 2025 – inadvertently showing how difficult it is to permanently alter car-centric infrastructure.


View image in fullscreen
Leopold’s Banchini’s project in Logroño only stood for a week. Photograph: Josema Cutillas
“If we had built something more permanent, we would have had to engage with safety concerns”, said Banchini, noting that bathers were only able to access the roundabout via a zebra crossing on one side.
“The rules around car traffic are hard to modify, and any requests usually go all the way up to municipal authorities”, he added. “And politicians are really scared to touch anything with cars, because they fear it will cost them in votes.”

Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice shared a Telegraph article headlined: "Heatwaves caused by fall in pollution." He said cleaner air, rather than carbon dioxide, was behind higher temperatures and claimed the public had been "gaslit".
He was wrong to suggest that carbon dioxide is not the primary driver of global warming. But the science he was distorting is real - and much more interesting than his original claim.
The fossil fuels that we've been burning for more than a century produce two very different kinds of pollution. As is well known, carbon dioxide warms the Earth. But less well-known is sulphur pollution, which forms vast numbers of tiny particles in the air and reflects sunlight back into space, partly counteracting the warming effect of carbon.
Thanks to clean-air policies around the world - like the US's Acid Rain Program in the early 1990s, that reduced gas pollution from power plants - sulphur emissions are falling sharply while carbon dioxide emissions remain near record highs.
Scientists increasingly believe the loss of that cooling effect is slightly speeding up global warming.


The past three years were the three warmest ever recorded, and the Met Office says 2027 is "very likely" to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record.














And away from social media, the argument over Tice's tweet raised an even more interesting - and worrying - question. Is it possible that our planet is actually more sensitive to greenhouse gases than we imagined?
And if so, might the climate be changing more rapidly than we feared?
Dust on the greenhouse
Global temperatures jump around naturally from year to year. El Niño, for example, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean, can temporarily push them higher. So a run of record hot years does not necessarily mean the underlying rate of global warming has increased.
Reto Knutti and his team at ETH Zurich have tried to strip out the effects of El Niño and other natural fluctuations to reveal the underlying trend.
"It's pretty clear that the rate of warming has accelerated," says Knutti, a professor of climate physics at the Swiss university and a former co-ordinating lead author for the IPCC - the UN-backed body that produces the world's most authoritative assessments of climate science.
A separate study published this year reached a similar conclusion after accounting for several major natural influences.
And it seems aerosols are playing a role.





Burning coal and oil releases sulphur dioxide, which forms tiny particles known as sulphate aerosols. These particles are bright and reflect some sunlight before it can reach and warm the planet's surface.

Stefania Di Bartolomeo was an early proponent of the environmental, social and governance (ESG) investing movement when she started Physis seven years ago. Her mission was to show just what companies were doing with the money investors gave them to fight climate change and encourage diversity – to bring transparency to sustainable investors. 
The Italian-born, Harvard-educated fund manager rode the wave of ESG in the early 2020s but then suffered, like many others, as President Donald Trump returned to the White House with a vow to stamp out climate change investing. Suddenly business was drying up and ESG was a banned word on Wall Street. Even worse for Di Bartolomeo, a few of her tech team staff from India were even stopped on the Harvard campus by ICE agents looking to expel immigrants.
The situation called for a turnaround, and so Di Bartolomeo embraced the AI movement and has spent the last year restructuring Physis into a data infrastructure business with a sustainability focus. A new website and platform are set to be launched this month, which importantly will allow the transparent data information the company had been selling to large investors to be available on a subscription level for smaller investors.




The new platform will also allow investors to build their own data bases to track the metrics of companies they invest in, including sustainable data but also other important financial, legal, and geographic information.

Land that borders a protected nature site is being investigated over claims it is being used as an illegal site to dump medical waste. 
The Environment Agency (EA) said it was investigating the site off Mill Lane, near Wadborough, in Worcestershire. The land is near Great Blaythorn Meadow, which is Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). 
A resident in the area, who asked not to be named, told the BBC a muck spreader, which are normally used to distribute farmyard manure, had been used to spread medical waste.
The EA said it was investigating alongside West Mercia Police, Wychavon District Council and Worcestershire County Council.
An EA spokesperson said: "Waste crime scars communities and the environment and, in line with our 10-point plan, we're acting quickly to tackle illegal activity."
The resident said they were concerned by how close the site was in relation to Great Blaythorn Meadow, which Natural England lists as an SSSI. 
Natural England considers the land special for its biological interest, specifically wanting to protect its rare lowland meadow and grassland habitat.

The Greens appeal to young and progressive voters here on defence, rent controls and North Sea oil. The Burnham bounce may be about to hit an obstacle





You might think a byelection showdown between two progressive parties is unimportant when the deep struggle for the national heart is between the right bloc and the left – but the result in Holborn and St Pancras matters. It matters for Andy Burnham and Labour because this is a test of the Burnham bounce: he saw off the right in Makerfield – can he win over the left too? Can he show he has enthusiastic approval from voters in southern constituencies as well as those in the north?
For the Greens it matters almost existentially because failing here could send them and their leader, Zack Polanski, back to the political fringes. Holborn and St Pancras, neighbouring Westminster, was vacated (vengefully) by Keir Starmer last week. This plum forever-Labour constituency has attracted 96 Labour applications for selection day on Wednesday, though not, it seems, nationally recognised names.



This is Labour’s to lose. And it might. The constituency was comfortably won in 2024 by Starmer; in May’s local elections the Greens took extra council seats, though Labour kept control and remained ahead by 10 percentage points. But byelections are idiosyncratic beasts in which voters risk nothing, electing neither council nor government. Few bother to turn out. For those who do, a byelection offers a free hit for whimsical preferences, “sending messages” on maverick issues or an urge to biff the government of the day.
A Labour loss would dent Burnham’s bounce, letting air out of his optimistic bubble. But frankly, losing here would be no great surprise. Peter Kellner, former president of YouGov and a leading psephologist, lives in this constituency, as do I. While most early opinion makes Labour the frontrunner, Kellner thinks that underestimates the byelection effect. He expects a Green win in a close call: “This is just the kind of seat a Labour government loses,” he tells me. In a metropolitan district with disproportionately young voters, the left is liberated to protest against anything disappointing in a Labour government.
Demographics favour rebellion for a rainbow of reasons in an extraordinarily socially mixed seat. You see vox-poppers choosing its picturesquely famous spots – the pastel houses in Primrose Hill where Paddington Bear lives in the films, the bars and cafes of Camden and Kentish Town – as photogenic backdrops to their reports. But, such elegant streets may be deceptive given that only a quarter of residents are homeowners, compared with 62.5% across England and Wales.


Here 43% live in social housing: Camden has a decades-long tradition of good housebuilding, thanks to a well-run council under great social pressure. The constituency is home to both deprivation and high numbers of graduates; many ABC1 voters and 45% born abroad.

French vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report a 30-year low in wine production after the country’s hottest ever recorded summer, according to the agriculture ministry.
Initial estimates suggest winemakers will produce just under 34m hectolitres from this year’s harvest: a drop of 6% on last year, and 17% less than ‌the 2021-2025 average.

Agreste, the government’s farming food, forestry and fishing statistics body, said the drop was partly caused by a reduction in the number and size of vineyards, but mostly the result of extreme weather conditions.
“The summer was particularly hot and dry: soil drought has intensified throughout the country and heatwaves have caused localised sun scald, scorching, defoliation, and wilting of the grapes, reducing harvest volumes,” it reported.


View image in fullscreen
A grape picker gets to work at the Trois Terres vineyard in Octon, southern France earlier this month. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA
However, some winemakers say with grape harvests still being conducted it is too early to make credible predictions.


The disappointing forecast comes after an optimistic start to the year, with heavy spring rains that encouraged grape growth. “The hot and dry summer conditions meant a deterioration of the [harvest] forecast,” Agreste reported.
A series of heatwaves brought the highest summer temperatures recorded in France since records began in 1900, with averages of 24C in June, July and August. Almost half of the country recorded temperatures on or above 40C.
Among the worst hit wine regions is Champagne where the grape harvest, which started unusually early in mid August, is predicted to be almost half that of last year. The Jura region in the east was the next worst hit with an estimated 37% loss. This year’s Burgundy-Beaujolais region grape production was expected to be one-third down, Agreste reported.
Winemakers in Bordeaux and the Languedoc-Roussillon as well as those in the south-east and south-west reported higher harvests this year but all except the Savoie region were down on the 2021-2025 five-year average for production.
However, Cécile Mathiaud of the Burgundy wine producers association said she was surprised by the government’s disastrous figures for her region’s vineyards.


“We know we won’t have a full harvest this year, but we have no definite figures and there’s no suggestion the situation is a disaster,” Mathiaud said. “We have some vineyards that have reported not much this year and others where it has been higher than expected.”

Some Burgundy vineyards began their harvest in early August but others are collecting the grapes now, she added. “Our reference is the historically low harvest of 2021 when we produced only 1m hectolitres; we think it will be higher this year, but the question is by how much? The company has seen sales fall in all of its major markets and has been dealing with the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year. 
At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future, in which it is likely to face intense competition from aggressively expanding Chinese brands. 
Executives have now decided a major overhaul is needed.
One of the main concerns for JLR is China. Not so long ago, it was seen as a land of opportunity for western carmakers, where the rapidly expanding middle classes seemed to have an inexhaustible appetite for upmarket foreign-badged vehicles. 
JLR, along with other European brands such as BMW, Audi and Mercedes Benz, was all too willing to meet that demand, at a time when the European market was extremely crowded and growth hard to find.
Today, things are very different. The past decade has seen rapid growth among domestic Chinese carmakers, firmly backed by their government, which has been determined to make the country a leading player in electric vehicles. 
This has created an environment of intense competition, in which local manufacturers have rapidly raised the bar in terms of technology and development speed.

That, combined with a slowdown in the Chinese economy and a reduction in sales overall, has made China a much more difficult market for European brands.
JLR's Chinese sales fell from a high water mark of 146,000 cars in 2017 to just 62,400 in the last financial year. At the same time, competition and a new luxury car tax have hit profit margins. 
All of this has resulted in a sharp fall in revenues from the region. JLR is not alone in this; the Volkswagen Group, for example, has also seen its earnings in China pummelled – a major factor in its decision to axe 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade.
The state of the Chinese market has had another consequence for European carmakers, including JLR. Faced with cut-throat competition at home, Chinese firms such as BYD and Chery have been flexing their muscles abroad. 
They have been rapidly gaining market share in the UK and Europe – with Chery's Jaecoo 7, nicknamed the 'Temu Range Rover' the third best-selling car in this country over the first half of the year. 
Analysts say traditional brands will face an uphill struggle to compete with new rivals, who can sell cars more cheaply and develop them more quickly.

Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.
The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.
JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.
Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.
"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.
JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.
The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save £1.7bn over the next two years.
JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.
He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack.
"It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.
Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.
In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.
In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to £22.9bn from £29bn in the previous two years.
Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.
"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.
He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party in terms of producing their first electric car which is just about to go into production".
Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".
The prime minister's official spokesman said: "We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities."

Heatwaves and wildfires are setting back air quality improvements, UN finds


WMO report details extreme weather events causing climatic feedback loop with serious health consequences




Big increases in wildfires and heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis are hindering improvements to air quality around the world, UN experts have said.
Regions that had recorded a fall in pollution emitted by cars and industrial sites are facing new threats to air quality because of exposure to smoke from wildfires, according to a new report, while rising temperatures caused by intense heatwaves are causing a surge in ground-level ozone.

In turn, the pollution generated by these climate-linked events is itself contributing to climate breakdown, creating a feedback loop that risks dragging the world deeper into environmental catastrophe.
“Air quality and climate cannot be treated as separate subjects; they are deeply intertwined and have to be treated together,” said Lorenzo Labrador, a scientific officer of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), which issued the report.


View image in fullscreen
Thick haze from expanding wildfires engulfs Palembang in South Sumatra. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA
The WMO publishes its air quality and climate bulletin annually, to coincide with the UN’s international day for clean air. Among its key findings was that extreme wildfires are increasing, leading to serious health consequences because of the toxicity of the smoke they are emitting.


This trend, “driven by a feedback loop between climate change and fire-conducive weather conditions”, was leading to an “urgent and growing public health threat”. As well as carrying high concentrations of fine particulate matter, smoke from wildfires causes oxidative stress in people’s bodies.
“Systematic reviews and experimental studies consistently link wildfire smoke exposure to increased asthma attacks, hospitalisations for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), spiked respiratory medication use, as well as impacts on mental health and birth outcomes,” the report said. According to one study cited, a tripling of wildfires since the 1990s had contributed to almost 100,000 deaths a year between 2010 and 2018.
The report also raises the alarm about ground-level ozone pollution, which is exacerbated by the kinds of intense and prolonged heatwaves that have affected Europe over this past summer.
“Ozone is a very powerful oxidant,” Labradorsaid. “So once it gets to the lung, it essentially oxidises lung tissue and causes inflammation and circulatory problems, and eventually heart problems.” In heavily polluted regions, roughly one in five deaths from COPD is now attributed to long-term exposure

We’re the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix. The heat crisis has us all facing the same question

Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate Gallego





Our three cities are learning from each other about how to protect residents. These climate policies are also public health measures





This summer, mayors met in London during the heatwave that ironically threatened to derail London Climate Action Week.
As temperatures broke records across the UK and Europe, leading some climate talks to be suspended or cancelled, we found ourselves seeking shelter and comparing how our cities prepare for extreme heat: how we protect vulnerable residents, communicate risk, and redesign neighbourhoods for hotter summers.

At the same time, Paris was overseeing the city’s crisis response as another intense heatwave swept across France. Across Europe, more than 14,000 people lost their lives due to the heat.
As mayors, we are confronting the same question: how do you protect millions of people when extreme heat is no longer an exceptional event, but an increasingly familiar part of summer?
For Phoenix, that question has shaped city government for decades. For Paris and Milan, it is now becoming one of the defining challenges of urban leadership.






Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster
Michael Mann

Read more
It may strike some people as unusual that two of Europe’s oldest and most prestigious cities are looking to a city in the Arizona desert for ideas. But rising temperatures are now a global challenge, and we don’t have time for each city to figure out what works on its own.
Phoenix has learned, sometimes the hard way, that extreme heat cannot be treated as simply a weather event. It shapes decisions about transport, housing, public health, public space, and emergency planning. Preparing for summer begins long before temperatures start to rise.


Phoenix established one of the world’s first city offices dedicated to heat response and mitigation, reflecting an approach that focuses on both immediate relief from extreme heat, especially for those most vulnerable, and building resilience in the medium-long-term by implementing cooling solutions to make the city safer and more comfortable.
The city’s shade plans require 75% shade coverage in new development in areas with high pedestrian activity, and programs that support schools, transit users, and those most vulnerable. To further reduce the urban heat island effect, Phoenix is applying cool surface treatment to buildings and roadways, including on more than 300 kilometers of neighborhood streets.

articles.jina_text:
The greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.
Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation over air conditioning.

If the atmosphere were to warm more than 3C above the average temperature in the preindustrial era, a prospect that looks ever more likely given the lackluster efforts to reduce carbon emissions, one in six of the world’s largest cities would suffer at least one heatwave per year lasting more than a month, according to the World Resources Institute. Low-income countries would suffer, on average, 6.9 heatwaves per year. Delhi would suffer at least 140 days with temperatures hitting at least 35C (95F).


Demand for AC around the world will inevitably accelerate as the atmosphere continues to warm. Ninety percent of households in the US and Japan enjoy artificial cooling. But in Indonesia, the share is only 9%. In India, it is 5%. Of the 2.8 billion people living in the hottest parts of the world, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), only 8% currently possess AC. These countries are populous, they are generally poorer and they will get particularly hot as climate change progresses.
The global stock of air conditioners in buildings is expected to mushroom to 5.6bn by 2050, up from 2.5bn today, according to the IEA. In India alone, installed AC inventory will rise from 48m units in 2020 to 1.1bn in 2050, a 23-fold increase. Even if the world met the emissions targets laid out in the 2015 Paris climate accords – which is not going to happen – an average of 40% to 50% of the population in many of the world’s warmest countries would still require AC.
This is going to require a lot of energy. Scientists at Harvard’s School of Engineering and applied sciences estimated that in India and Indonesia, demand for power just for cooling in 2050 could be as high as 75% of their current total annual electricity demand.
This poses a challenge for the climate. In 2022, energy for cooling, mostly for residential and nonresidential space cooling but also to maintain cold chains for food and pharmaceutical production, and to cool transport, accounted for roughly 2.5bn tons of CO2 equivalent emissions, according to a United Nations report, about 7% of total emissions. In the absence of further strategies to improve energy efficiency and improve passive cooling techniques, it would rise to nearly 8bn tons by 2050.

As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.
What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.
The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.
The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.
Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.
He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.
"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.
"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes with… to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".

articles.jina_text:
Donald Trump has signed an executive order to remove endangered species protection for the grey wolf and a subspecies, the Mexican wolf.
The US president's decision could pave the way for pastoral farmers to kill the canines to protect their livestock. His order said ranchers played a "vital role" in the food supply chain and American cultural heritage.
But conservation groups have criticised the move, saying it could derail long-term efforts to recover the endangered wolf populations.
There were 319 Mexican wolves in the wild in the US in 2025, up from just four when they were reintroduced in 1998, US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) figures show. 
Meanwhile, there are roughly 18,000 grey wolves across the US, though they are still considered endangered as most of their habitat has been destroyed by humans.
An attempt to de-list them at a federal level in 2022 became tied up in litigation, and some campaigners have indicated they intend to do the same of the US Department of Interior acts on Trump's order.
The executive order does not give ranchers immediate license to shoot wolves preying on livestock, but instead gives Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to determine whether the grey and Mexican wolf populations had recovered enough to warrant being taken off the endangered species list.
Noting that US livestock herds were at a 75-year low while demand for beef had risen by 10% in the past decade, the order added: "More can and should be done to support this critical industry."





Advertisement












However, environmental groups pointed to studies that suggested wolf attacks on livestock were rare and had little impact on ranchers' income.
"This is a huge distraction to placate a handful of ranchers and make them believe that wolves are a greater threat than President Trump's own policies," said Greta Anderson, deputy director of Western Watersheds Project, which works to conserve wildlife in western US states.
The Wolf Conservation Center noted that ranchers were entitled to up to 100% compensation for any livestock losses caused by wolves under the current system, with individual states providing funding for programmes to deter attacks.
"The Mexican grey wolf is not recovered simply because the population has grown," said Claire Musser, executive director of the Grand Canyon Wolf Recovery Project. "Weakening federal protections now would put decades of recovery work at risk."
The executive order comes as the Trump administration is seeking to lower record-high beef prices for consumers, driven by drought and an outbreak of parasites in US beef stocks.
Ranchers have been frustrated by Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on beef imports to address price rises, putting pressure on their already tight margins.

articles.jina_text:
Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the interior department to consider de-listing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act and to contemplate whether the agency could make it easier to authorize killing them.
The order gives interior secretary Doug Burgum three months to determine whether gray wolves and Mexican gray wolves have recovered enough for the federal government to de-list them.

But the US Fish and Wildlife Service, a division of the interior department, has already attempted to de-list the gray wolf – a decision that is currently tied up in litigation. A 2022 federal court order has left wolves protected by the ESA across most of their range in the lower 48 states.
The major exception is in the northern Rocky Mountain states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming, where states manage wolves. In Minnesota, wolves are classified as “threatened” rather than “endangered”.
The USFWS has not attempted to de-list the Mexican gray wolf, a rare sub-species that was reintroduced to New Mexico and Arizona in 1998.
The current recovery plan for Mexican gray wolves requires a population average of more than 320 animals for four years in a row before federal authorities consider de-listing. Arizona and New Mexico counted a total of 319 animals at the end of 2025, triggering the first year in which officials can start counting to make the case for de-listing.

The Met Office has warned the El Niño event developing over the Pacific is shaping up to be the most significant in living memory - and it will impact the weather in London over the coming months.




Forecasters have said that the phenomenon will cause the UK to experience more storms and rain over the coming autumn and winter.








It comes as Britons have been urged to stock up on food and water as the government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for emergencies. 




Environment secretary Angela Eagle told the Guardian: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.




“If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”




An El Niño event is declared when sea surface temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise to 0.5C above the long-term average, impacting global rainfall patterns and average temperatures.












Current measurements show that they are over 2C above normal - and the Met Office is predicting that it could measure over 3C more than average later this year.




That would make this year’s weather event the largest since at least 1950, and possibly since the 19th century, according to the national forecaster.








Other climate groups have projected temperatures to even reach 4C above average.

How will El Niño impact London’s weather?




The impact of such an event would mean that London, along with all of northwest Europe, would experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter.




El Niño can also increase the odds of cold weather late in the winter.




Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the Met Office, said: “We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”

articles.raw_rss: Experts said the drop on the Isle of May in the Firth of Forth is ‘disappointing’.

articles.jina_text:
The number of puffins at one of the UK’s largest colonies has fallen by about 30% in the last two years, raising concerns for their future amid climate change.




Experts fear “extreme climate events”, including intense storms and marine heat waves, have had an impact on the birds’ survival rates in recent years.








NatureScot and the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) completed a count of burrows at the Isle of May National Nature Reserve (NNR) in the Firth of Forth this summer.




Scientists estimate that 36,500 puffin burrows were occupied, compared to 52,000 in the last survey in 2024, and 39,000 in 2017.


Puffins spend up to eight months of the year at sea (Owen Humphreys/PA)
PA Archive




NatureScot Isle of May reserve manager, David Steel, said: “This decline is disappointing and concerning.




“Puffin numbers on the island fell sharply in the 2000s and recovered in the 2010s but have now dropped again.




“The decrease appears to be linked to a combination of ongoing pressures on seabird food supplies, poor winter survival and increasingly extreme weather conditions.












“Unfortunately, this mirrors similar challenges that are affecting seabirds more widely.




“All of this underlines the importance of continued monitoring and conservation work at sites like the Isle of May NNR, where data and research are playing a vital role in helping us to understand these trends and respond.”




Puffins can spend up to eight months of the year out at sea, and only return to land in early spring to breed.








The birds generally mate for life, and pairs often return each year to the same nesting spot where the female lays a single egg which hatches into a puffling.


Rising ocean temperatures can affect the availability of food sources (Niall Carson/PA)
PA Archive




UKCEH said its long-term research shows that puffins have struggled with the impacts of climate change.

Storms in recent years have killed large numbers of birds, while rising ocean temperatures can reduce the availability of food sources for puffins – particularly sandeels.




UKCEH has been monitoring seabird colonies on the Isle of May for five decades.




Mark Newell, UKCEH’s field manager on the Isle of May, said: “We believe that the puffin population has recently suffered from a series of extreme climate events, including marine heat waves and intense storms affecting survival in three of the last five winters.












“The concern for puffins and other seabirds is that climate scientists are predicting an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme events in future.”

It’s the end of summer and Kemi Badenoch chose to mark the occasion with a reshuffle of her shadow cabinet. Her aim is apparently to get the Tories match fit in case Andy Burnham calls an early general election, but the vibes are much more rearranging the deckchairs on a sinking ship. After all, when the gene pool of talent is that small, there’s not much you can do. James Cleverly got the ball rolling by announcing he was planning to be the Conservative candidate for London mayor in two years’ time. He may have his work cut out. London is a liberal, multicultural city and unlikely to be won over by a party giving up on net zero and the European convention on human rights.

Cleverly’s replacement as shadow housing secretary is Katie Lam, who was only elected two years ago but has been desperate to attract attention by consistently saying the most offensive thing she can think of. Fashion has become remarkably skilled at presenting small improvements as systemic change. A garment made with recycled fibres, a lower-impact collection or a resale scheme may suggest progress, yet the industry continues to manufacture clothes in quantities the planet cannot sustain.
For Safia Minney, the pioneering ethical fashion entrepreneur who founded People Tree and went on to establish Fashion Declares, and Indilisi incremental improvements are no longer enough. A genuine response to the climate crisis requires the industry to confront a far more difficult question: how can fashion produce dramatically fewer clothes without abandoning the millions of workers whose livelihoods depend upon making them?

Such a contraction would represent far more than a change in seasonal trends or consumer habits. It would fundamentally reshape a global industry built on speed, volume and cheap labour. Factories would receive fewer orders and jobs would disappear, many of them in countries where garment work provides a vital, if often precarious, source of income.
“Obviously, what that means is that a lot of people will lose their jobs in fashion supply chains,” Minney says.

articles.jina_text:
An unprecedented El Nino event – when sea temperatures in tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the long-term average – is forecast to reach more than 3C in the coming months, making this year’s event “the largest since the 19th century”, according to the Met Office.








El Nino creates a heightened risk of drought in the tropics, southern Africa and north-east Australia, while north-western Europe – including the UK – is likely to experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter, the forecaster said.




Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle has urged people to store supplies in case of extreme weather events.




And the Environment Secretary said people in the UK should prepare for the increased risk of national weather emergencies.




She told The Guardian: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Nino that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.




“It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.




“If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t.











“So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”


Dame Angela Eagle has encouraged people to prepare (PA)
PA Wire




Professor Bill McGuire, professor emeritus of geophysical hazards, University College London, last month said the Met Office and other scientific forecasts “suggest that the world is in for one hell of a ride”.




“The astonishing and unprecedented amount of heat building across the eastern Pacific Ocean is all but certain to make this the most powerful El Nino in living memory – possibly even the biggest in several centuries,” he said.

Major Australian alpine resorts are closing their ski operations up to a month early after a winter that broke multiple records for heat with limited snow falls being washed away by rain.
Predictions in June that a building El Niño could combine with global heating for a challenging ski season came to pass, with seven resorts either already closed or announcing ski lifts will stop operating this weekend.

This week the Victorian resorts of Mount Buller, Mount Hotham and Falls Creek, together with Charlotte Pass in New South Wales, all announced ski operations would end this weekend.
The Victorian resort of Mount Baw Baw, the NSW resort at Selwyn and Tasmania’s Ben Lomond have already closed. Resorts typically aim to stay open until the first weekend of October.
 
 


Resorts blamed “challenging” weather conditions and lack of snowfall. Two other major NSW resorts at Perisher and Thredbo remain open.
“The season was frankly a shocker. This was the fourth disappointing season since 2020,” said Dr Andrew Watkins, a climate scientist and adjunct professor at the Monash University and a science adviser to the campaign group Protect our Winters.
“The problems were El Niño and climate change. It was not that dry this year, but the problem was the warmth. The heat just did us in.”
Watkins, who is also a keen skier, said winter temperatures had been too high and precipitation that might have fallen as snow, had instead fallen as rain.
“Rain is the natural enemy of a snowpack. It melts it and then washes it away,” he said.

Data from the Bureau of Meteorology show Falls Creek and Mount Hotham had their wettest winters in more than 30 years but, together with Mount Buller, they also had their warmest winters on record for average maximum and minimum temperatures.
Watkins said data from weather observations at Cabramurra in Kosciuszko national park suggested alpine winters had warmed by about 2C since the 1960s.
He said that temperature rise would have been the difference between precipitation falling as rain instead of snow. “It would have been a bumper season if it had been 50 years ago,” he said.
The El Niño currently in place in the Pacific Ocean can promote hotter and drier temperatures in Australia’s south-east in winter and spring.
This week the bureau forecast the current El Niño would be the strongest on record and Australian scientists said climate change had made the strength of the event six times more likely.

articles.jina_text:
More than half (53%) of Northern Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in the year to June – beating the level previously set in 2022.
And for the first time renewable generation has consistently exceeded non-renewable generation since January.
Even when imported electricity was taken into account, the amount of renewables equalled the previous record of 50%, set in 2022/23.
The Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the increasing level of renewable energy would help Northern Ireland "move away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices" .
Almost three-quarters (74%) of renewable electricity came from wind. Bioenergy – anaerobic digestion, incineration and fermentation – provided just under one-fifth (18%).
Solar energy provided 6%, landfill gas provided 1%, and hydro/tidal generation provided 1%.
Northern Ireland has a target of generating 80% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030.
The increase to 53% to June 2026 follows several years of reduced renewable generation.














Lower levels can be due to weather conditions.
There is also a high rate of dispatch down in Northern Ireland – when turbines are switched off because there is not enough demand for the power being generated.
That is to protect the grid which has a limit on the amount of renewable energy it can carry due to fluctuations.
But moving to more renewable energy is a critical part of the journey to net zero and the transition from fossil fuels.
The minister said the rising cost of fossil fuels globally was "impacting negatively" on both businesses and households, particularly those with lower incomes.
She added that increased levels of renewable electricity "move us away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices for the electricity we use".

Exclusive: Angela Eagle urges UK citizens to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as they plan for national emergencies




British people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide.
Forecasters say they are braced for the biggest El Niño in 1,000 years, bringing wildfires and floods to parts of the world, and the threat of a wet, stormy winter for the UK.

 As the British government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for national emergencies, Angela Eagle told the Guardian the likelihood of a wild winter showed the importance of keeping supplies at home.

The environment secretary said: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

 “It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

 “If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”


El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.
The most recent data, from Monday, shows the temperature of the ocean at the heart of El Niño at 2.6C above the 30-year average. That is already close to the highest anomaly ever recorded in the satellite data era, 3.1C in 2015, with months to go before the peak is expected.
That peak is forecast to reach about 4C in November, according to the average of 14 different models. Zeke Hausfather, a climate analyst, said data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggested no El Niño had reached this level in the last millennium. Any temperature anomaly above 0.5C is classed as an El Niño.
The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be the hottest year ever recorded.

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates 
 




The growing El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east is already breaking heat records, with forecasts showing it may easily surpass previous events, according to Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology.
Separate research suggests climate change has greatly shortened the odds of the event hitting record extremes.

On Thursday, the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”







‘Supersizing before our eyes’: UN warns of record El Niño approaching

In an update this week, the Bureau of Meteorology said the El Niño was now forecast to peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”.
El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires.
El Niño strength is assessed by analysing sea surface temperatures in a region of the equatorial Pacific known as Niño 3.4. The bureau has said the strength of an El Niño does not necessarily mean stronger effects for the continent.

Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region for the month of August were likely to be between 2.2C and 2.3C above average – higher than any previous August since 1950 (the year after which records are considered to be more reliable).
